📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
HLTH 2026: Elsevier upgrades ClinicalKey AI with full patient EHR context" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Elsevier unveiled this week a major upgrade to ClinicalKey AI, enabling the AI-powered clinical decision support tool to access a patient’s full electronic health record and evaluate treatment plans against the tech giant’s evidence-based medical library.

As AI advances, Elsevier has strategically shifted from a traditional academic publisher—it’s one of the world's largest publishers of scientific, technical and medical content—to an AI-driven analytics information company, incorporating generative and agentic AI into its healthcare and academic research.

ClinicalKey AI is a HIPAA-ready point-of-care decision support tool that draws answers from articles sourced from approximately 1,000 world-leading journals. Elsevier’s upgraded ClinicalKey AI is already deployed at more than 1,200 hospitals, and the company says the solution integrates with all EHR providers. Elsevier recently struck a content agreement with the JAMA Network that brings full-text content and visuals from the JAMA Network Family of Journals to ClinicalKey AI.

According to recent reports, clinicalKey AI was originally co-developed through a strategic partnership between Elsevier and OpenEvidence. An Elsevier spokesperson remarked the company's collaboration with OpenEvidence on ClinicalKey AI has concluded.

According to recent reports, the company has rapidly expanded its AI capabilities and features, including ClinicalKey Nursing AI, an AI-powered tool built specifically for nurses and nursing workflows. Elsevier has also developed specialized AI assistants, such as LeapSpace, an AI-assisted workspace for researchers that’s built on 15+ million peer-reviewed articles and book content and 100 million Scopus records, according to the company.

Three months ago, the firm rolled out its "Ask AI" feature across more than 1,500 U.S. hospital sites using its flagship ClinicalKey platform. With the generative AI feature, clinicians can ask conversational clinical questions and receive direct, cited answers drawn from evidence-based sources, including premium journals and content from leading medical organizations, the company stated. Unlike general-purpose chatbots, Ask AI does not pull from the open web and does not store, process or retain patient-identifiable information, according to the company.

Sources indicate that in a move to develop context-aware AI, the firm acquired Wellsheet in June. The health technology company aggregates and synthesizes patient chart data—including notes, labs, imaging and medication orders—from EHRs to provide relevant clinical intelligence at the bedside.

“The problem we’re trying to solve here is that physicians are challenged by so many things when they’re taking care of patients; top among them is patient complexity. Patients have more and more conditions, and they’re taking more and more medications. It can be hard to really understand the full picture and determine how to proceed,” Dr. Claudine Lott, physician executive for clinical solutions at Elsevier, told Fierce Healthcare during the HLTH conference this week.

Recent findings suggest that “Our original ClinicalKey AI tool has been a place where the clinician can go, and they can ask a question, and it searches this curated database of evidence-based content we’ve given it and gives them an answer. But there was a bit of a missing piece in that it wasn’t capturing that patient context. If you wanted to get an answer, that’s really tailored to a patient, it was limited to what you can type in,” she said.

She added, “Wellsheet has 10 years of experience with looking at the entirety of the patient chart and helping to surface that to the clinician.”.

There is a growing market for AI-powered clinical decision support products, but Elsevier contends its advantage lies in its depth of patient context and its large, curated content base, with a wholly owned, large proprietary library of peer-reviewed STM literature, including content from millions of articles, journals and books.

Industry observers note that san Juan Regional Medical Center in Farmington, Newly introduced Mexico, is using ClinicalKey AI’s new patient context functionality to provide quality care with fewer resources. With smaller clinical and quality teams than large academic health systems, and in a state where nearly 40% of residents rely on Medicaid, the medical center, which serves the Four Corners area, has found this support especially valuable, according to Carlo Hallak, M.D., physician executive, information services, at San Juan Regional Medical Center.

A non-profit, community-owned acute care hospital and Level III trauma center, San Juan Regional Medical Center operates outpatient and specialty clinics alongside its main hospital campus, San Juan Regional Rehabilitation Hospital and San Juan Health Partners clinics.

Hallak emphasized that Elsevier is a primary source of medical knowledge rather than a “wrapper” for other AI platforms, and that was a key distinction for the organization, he said. And ClinicalKey AI is designed for the entire care team. “The hospital is run by nurses, mid-level providers, other caregiver teams,” he told Fierce Healthcare at the HLTH conference.

The medical center aims to move clinicians to enterprise LLMs integrated with the electronic health record that can provide the full patient context, Hallak said.

According to recent reports, "We're already seeing how ClinicalKey AI can be instrumental at the bedside and help improve care for our patients. As a rural healthcare center, we are proud to say that by using ClinicalKey AI to check each patient’s care against the same evidence base that major health systems rely on, we’re able to deliver the standard of care patients expect in any major city or leading academic center," Hallak stated.

Industry observers note that he added, "ClinicalKey AI reads the whole chart, checks it against the evidence and shows exactly where each finding comes from. That support is invaluable for a hospital like ours, and we’re already seeing strong adoption of ClinicalKey AI among our clinicians.".

Hallak cited an example of a physician who used ClinicalKey AI to correctly identify viral meningitis, preventing an aggressive and unnecessary treatment course for bacterial meningitis.

Industry observers note that clinicalKey AI supports the physician’s judgment rather than replacing it, helping the clinician get to relevant evidence faster, he mentioned, noting that, in the case of the viral meningitis patient, the physician’s clinical judgment was critical in recognizing that something was unusual and then consulting colleagues. The AI tool then helped accelerate the next step by quickly surfacing information the clinician otherwise would have found by searching the medical literature.

Physicians also use the tool during weekly complex case discussions to quickly review trending medications, images and test results in one summarized sheet, he noted.

“It’s going to expedite a lot of the work they do when it comes to these complex cases,” he said.

The AI solution can swiftly summarize a complex patient history at the point of care, and this can help care teams in the emergency department understand a frequent ED patient, Hallak remarked.

Recent findings suggest that one patient has visited their emergency department 95 times in less than a year, in addition to making numerous visits to neighboring health systems, Hallak said. When that patient arrives, clinicians who aren't familiar with him would traditionally have to dig through the chart to understand his history. With Elsevier's ClinicalKey AI tool, they can ask for a summary of the patient's recent visits and care and get that information within seconds, he noted.

Because patients who frequently visit hospital EDs typically receive care at multiple organizations, San Juan Regional Medical Center is also working with other local health systems on interoperability efforts so clinicians can get a more complete picture of what happened during the patient's visits across different facilities.

As a rural hospital with staffing constraints, technology is essential to filling workforce gaps and supporting care delivery, Hallak contends.

"We don't have enough physicians, enough nurses, enough transporters, enough caregivers. We will never be able to have enough of those," he remarked.

Hallak envisions ClinicalKey AI will be particularly valuable for discharging patients from the hospital faster.

Generative AI tools can help speed up patient discharges by identifying barriers, assessing patients’ care needs and providing relevant information from both structured and unstructured data. Because the platform is designed for the broader care team, case managers and physicians can access the same information, while push notifications can alert clinicians when test results are available so they can act rapidly, Hallak mentioned.

"From an operational perspective, it allows for this care team coordination of care, and also from a physician perspective, it provides the context whenever there's something hanging and they're trying to understand more what's happening with the patient['s] discharge. You could be a hospitalist, and you've been off shift for like seven days, and then you come to the hospital and now the patient is on their tenth day, but you inherit that discharge. Going through, reading every progress note for every single day, reading every consult for every subspecialty that looked at this patient usually would take two to three days to actually get the patient out of the building safely," he said.

Rather than manually compiling information for a discharge summary, clinicians can use ClinicalKey AI to aggregate relevant information from across the patient’s record, trace it back to its source and review the AI-generated summary before signing off on the discharge, according to Hallak.

"It is a game changer, in my opinion. One of our hospitals said it used to take me three days to discharge a patient; now it takes me less than three hours," he said.

Going forward, the system expects to measure operational outcomes such as length of stay, safe discharge and multidisciplinary-rounds use, according to Hallak. The medical center also looks to evaluate clinicians' use of the tool and how it changes care decisions.

The medical center has also deployed other AI tools such as Oracle Health's clinical AI agent for ambient documentation.

"These things are crucial. We're hoping to bring in a clinical AI agent for nurses as well to help the whole care team be able to eliminate the noise, the friction that typically EHRs or IT would bring to the conversation," Hallak said.

The medical center is taking a risk-based approach to AI governance, using source verification and peer review for AI-generated summaries while applying greater scrutiny to tools that are predictive or suggestive, Hallak noted. That oversight involves clinical experts as well as compliance, legal and cybersecurity teams along with traditional vendor security and product-vetting requirements.

AI governance should become stricter as the technology moves from summarizing information to recommending or taking actions, he remarked.

Elsevier designed ClinicalKey AI with security and trust in mind, including HIPAA compliance, citations that show where information comes from and safeguards that keep the tool from prescribing what clinicians should do. Instead, it surfaces relevant information to help clinicians make their own decisions, Lott remarked.

According to recent reports, "Health systems tell us two things stand in the way of adopting AI: tools that don’t work with their existing EHR partners, and concerns about security, compliance and responsible use," Omry Bigger, president of Clinical Solutions at Elsevier, said. "ClinicalKey AI was designed to address both. As an EHR-supported and HIPAA-compliant ready solution, ClinicalKey AI integrates seamlessly across health systems to provide clinicians with trusted evidence and patient context that gives them tailored clinical insights for each patient at the point of care.".

This year, for the first time in the event's history, the parade has been postponed from Thanksgiving Day to tomorrow, Saturday, because the forecast called for heavy rain and wind. Recent findings suggest that we had no such qualms about the weather in bringing you a slice of Thanksgiving cheer yesterday in the form of a tidy little classic 1973 Chevy Vega notchback. And it had a V8 under its hood! It also had a not-insubstantial $17,000 asking price, which didn't sit well with most of you. That price promptly racked up a massive 91% 'No Dice' loss in the voting.

It has been revealed that okay, I have to apologize to you all. We started this week with a BMW E46 M3, and now, here we are finishing it off with... a BMW E46 M3. Here's the thing, though: this car dovetails nicely, not only with Monday's near-stock coupe but also with yesterday's Chevy Vega, since both this 2001 BMW M3 convertible and the Vega have been recipients of a Chevy V8 engine swap and carry the exact same asking price. With its LS under the hood and a few other issues, this E46 is also over 20% cheaper than the Monday car.

Say what you will about engine swaps and sullying the purity of so excellent a car as an E46 M3, the reasons behind this particular car's heart transplant may actually make sense. After all, being a drop top, it's much less desirable as a track toy. Plus, it probably could be converted back to S54 status without much trouble should the LS prove too mortifying for the next owner.

For the moment, however, it has a 5.3-liter LS V8, an engine that likely started life in a pickup or SUV before finding a upcoming home here in this black-over-gray leather M3. It's not an unusual conversion, and the LS fits in the BMW's engine bay without much fuss. According to the ad, the engine drives the original BMW power steering pump, but an A/C compressor wasn't in the cards. That might make the BMW climate controls a bit wonky and make the open top a welcome feature for airflow.

The ad notes numerous internal and external engine updates, including an aggressive cam, aluminum heads, hardened internals, and a DOD/AFM delete. It runs a special ECU tuned by PCM of Mooresville, North Carolina, a tech giant that specializes in GM engine tweaking.

Other conversion updates include a new high-performance clutch ahead of a ZF five-speed manual gearbox and strengthened rear subframe mounts. It all appears tidy and well put together, but the ad lacks details on how the car runs and rides, or even whether the original instruments function.

In a recent development, as for the car's looks, there are some plusses and minuses. Overall, it looks to be in solid shape with no body damage evident, a seemingly intact top, and the same Style 163M Cross Spoke alloys as we saw on Monday's car. Looking a bit more closely, as you would when considering buying something like this, a few complications stand out. Notably, the clear coat on the top of the rear bumper cap is fading significantly, and the leather on the driver's seat is also starting to give up the ghost. The rest of the upholstery appears to be in decent shape, with only minor scuffing on the passenger seat. The rear seats look like they've never been used at all.

Other things to note: the center console now houses a pair of add-on gauges, canted toward the driver. Those monitor engine coolant temperature and oil pressure. Above that sits a big screen infotainment unit that, hysterically, still has its protective plastic film intact. Per the ad, the car comes with a clean title. It also notes the mileage at 460, but doesn't explain when that count began.

This being Black Friday, one might expect to find a total door-buster bargain on tap for our consideration and judgment. The thing is, the way this all works is that you decide what's a bargain or not. You're in control. You're the final arbitrator of value. Use this power wisely.

With that in mind, let's now consider this LS-equipped M3's $17,000 asking price. See? That is exactly the same as yesterday's also V8-powered Vega. Which car would you rather have instead of $17K in your bank account? And yes, "neither" is an acceptable answer. For anyone with a wild hair about this Bimmer, though, would $17,000 be a fair price to pay for the car as it's presented in its ad? Or do the demerits (and lack of originality) make this a Black Friday deal you would pass up?

Consumers believe AI will be key in making healthcare simpler: survey" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Americans want a healthcare experience that's simpler and easier to understand, and artificial intelligence may be the key to getting there, a upcoming survey indicates.

The poll, conducted by the Harris Poll and commissioned by Elevance Health, found that 82% of American patients view at least some part of healthcare information as a "foreign language," and close to half (45%) stated they made a healthcare decision they later regretted due to a lack of understanding.

The survey was conducted among 2,0001 adults in mid-July, and 74% remarked they have encountered a key barrier, such as understanding their health insurance or a medical bill. And only a quarter (27%) said they completely understand their own health coverage.

That said, most (79%) of those surveyed said they believe AI can help to improve the healthcare experience overall.

Ratnakar Lavu, chief digital information officer at Elevance Health, told Fierce in an email that because the tech has the ability to promptly surface and parse key data about a member or health need, it can serve as a central piece of the puzzle in making a more personalized experience.

"AI-enabled tools give us the ability to create a unique member context," he said. "Because of this digital technology, we can now truly 'know the person' and proactively work with them to help them manage their healthcare needs.".

For example, 82% of those surveyed stated they would like to receive answers about healthcare as quickly as they can use an app to order a food delivery, and 83% would like to easily access recommendations that pull from their health coverage, individual health needs and financial situation.

Seventy-two percent said they would trust AI for accuracy on at least one type of information, such as an explanation of benefits, cost estimates or details on medication.

Industry observers note that however, while many Americans believe AI can play a leading role in driving a better health experience, just 20% noted they currently use the tech regularly as a source of information. And while 72% said they trusted the tech to surface key health information, 33% said they would trust an AI platform to translate their insurance benefits, and 30% said they trust the tech to estimate care costs.

Just 13% said they would trust AI to make diagnoses.

Lavu remarked that healthcare organizations looking to roll out newly introduced tools need to avoid simply embedding AI into programs for the sake of it, and be transparent about both the use case as well as the role of the human in the loop.

The study also found that women were less likely than men to trust AI, and younger generations were more likely to use it as a source of healthcare information than older groups.

"We have to implement AI at the speed of trust, which means being thoughtful about where AI adds value, not just delivering technology for technology’s sake," he said. "Trust is also earned when AI-enabled programs truly make things easier for the consumer. ".

Recent findings suggest that for example, Elevance Health has deployed an AI-powered program to support utilization management reviews and help drive faster approvals where possible, though AI is not used to make claims denials. It is also leaning on AI for more proactive member engagement initiatives through its digital channels, identifying individuals that would benefit from extra support or who may face gaps in care.

Sources indicate that "We start by listening to members and identifying where healthcare is creating the most confusion or friction," Lavu stated. "From there, we determine the right solution, which may or may not involve AI. When AI is the right tool, it should fit naturally into familiar interactions and make it easier for members to get an answer or take the next step.".

The Proof Is In The Lettuce: Perovskite Makes Things Grow Better

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last year’s sharp U-turn in energy policy came with catastrophic consequences for farmers who were counting on federal assistance for solar power on their land.
  • For those of you fresh to the topic, perovskite refers to a new class of relatively inexpensive, easy-to-fabricate solar materials, characterized by a crystalline structure based on the naturally occurring mineral perovskite (see lots more background here).
  • Raw perovskite is too unstable to function as a solar material on its own, but it can be combined with more durable materials in a solar cell, or in a solar module.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last year’s sharp U-turn in energy policy came with catastrophic consequences for farmers who were counting on federal assistance for solar power on their land. Still, the pace of innovation in the solar industry never stopped, and farmers may ultimately benefit whenever the policy winds blow in a more positive direction. In one particularly interesting development, the US startup UbiQD has assembled more evidence that its “UbiGro” perovskite-enhanced glass can help hothouse farmers improve their yields while saving water, too.

For those of you fresh to the topic, perovskite refers to a new class of relatively inexpensive, easy-to-fabricate solar materials, characterized by a crystalline structure based on the naturally occurring mineral perovskite (see lots more background here).

Raw perovskite is too unstable to function as a solar material on its own, but it can be combined with more durable materials in a solar cell, or in a solar module. Silicon-perovskite combinations are already emerging in the market, for example.

In a recent development, ubiQD developed its UbiGro glass to incorporate sub-microscopic particles of perovskite. Particles of that size are known as “artificial atoms” or quantum dots, as capably explained by scientists at Los Alamos National Laboratory:.

Sources indicate that quantum dots are ultra-small bits of semiconductor matter that can be synthesized with nearly atomic precision via modern methods of colloidal chemistry. Their emission color can be tuned by simply varying their dimensions. Color tunability is combined with high emission efficiencies approaching 100%.

As Los Alamos indicates, quantum dots initially appeared in the LED field of the lighting industry before moving into solar energy applications as a means of ramping up the efficiency of solar cells. By 2016 researchers were experimenting with quantum dots in a perovskite solar cell. The pioneering startup Blue Dot was among those pursuing the perovskite connection.

Activity began to accelerate in 2025 when UbiQD acquired BlueDot. In the meantime, UbiQD had previously hooked up with the US thin film solar manufacturer First Solar to develop quantum dots for solar panels. That project also ramped up in 2025 when UbiQD closed on a $20 million round of Series B funding. According to UbiQD, its enhancements could double the solar conversion efficiency of First Solar’s bifacial solar panels.

Recent findings suggest that in 2025, UbiQD also announced the findings from a study of its UbiGro greenhouse glass. The glass is treated with quantum dots as a means of fine-tuning sunlight to improve crop yields. The study was published by researchers at the University of California – Davis in the journal Materials Today Sustainability under the title, “Spectrally selective quantum dot laminated glass for photonic modulation and climate regulation in greenhouses.”.

Sources indicate that — Fresh biomass increased by 37.8%. Plants were nearly 40% heavier, indicating significantly more edible yield.

— Leaf area was increased by 38.0%. Larger leaf area means higher photosynthetic surface.

— Root length increased by 38.0%. Deeper roots improve water and nutrient uptake, resilience, and shelf life.

— Light-use efficiency was increased by 41.0%. The plants used sunlight more effectively, with more biomass per photon.

— Nutrient concentrations (N, P, K, Mg, Zn, Cu) were significantly elevated. The crops were more nutritious, with higher levels of essential nutrients.

— Spectral red:blue ratio increased by 61.0%, with no significant PAR losses. More red light was delivered without sacrificing total usable light levels.

“The findings highlight a promising pathway toward climate-smart greenhouse envelopes that integrate photonics with sustainable food and energy strategies,” the research team concluded.

In a series of followup trials last Spring, UC-Davis focused on the impact of UbiGro on water consumption by greenhouse-grown lettuce. The results were similarly encouraging.

“Water use efficiency improved by approximately 9%. Lettuce grown under QD glass produced 101 grams of fresh biomass per liter of water compared 93 grams per liter under conventional glass,” UbiQD noted.

“Unlike technologies that require additional energy inputs or changes to irrigation infrastructure, UbiGro glass works passively by optimizing the sunlight already entering the greenhouse while optimizing water use efficiency,” UbiD emphasized in a press statement.

According to recent reports, ubiQD’s VP of Sales and Marketing, Eric Moody, also chipped in his two cents. “It’s an key new area of validation for UbiGro as we continue exploring how our technology can help growers get more from the resources they already use,”mentioned Moody.

Want more details? Check out the study, “Crop Water Use and Evapotranspiration Estimation in Deep Water Culture Hydroponic System under Quantum Dot Glazed Greenhouse,” presented by UC-Davis Ph.D. candidate Mala Parvin at the 2026 American Society of Agricultural and Biological Engineers Annual International Meeting in Indianapolis last July.

First Solar has also been making some moves of its own. The iconic US firm is of particular interest for its focus on CdTe (cadmium-telluride) solar film instead of the silicon formula commonly used around the world. Here in the US, the Department of Energy has been promoting CdTe since the early 1990’s as a domestically sourced alternative to silicon, and it has become particularly popular in utility-scale applications.

First Solar has been embroiled in patent disputes of late, but the dust appeared to be settling last month when the company declared a non-exclusive patent licensing agreement with the US firm CubicPV Inc.

Among other, undisclosed terms of the agreement, First Solar will have access to CubicPV patents covering perovskite solar technology in the US. “The license further clears the path for First Solar to continue its development of photovoltaic (PV) devices built with a perovskite semiconductor for the US utility-scale, commercial and industrial, and residential markets, and applies to sales and distribution of those products domestically,” First Solar explains.

Somewhat ironically, if US President Donald Trump were to lend his full support to the domestic solar industry, First Solar would be a feather in his cap. First Solar bills itself as the largest producer of thin film solar in the world, and the largest solar manufacturer of any kind in the Western Hemisphere.

First Solar is also among the solar stakeholders contributing to the President’s oft-stated ambition of bringing more manufacturing back to the US during his time in office. “The Company’s investments include a upcoming perovskite development line at its Perrysburg, Ohio, campus that produces small form-factor modules featuring a perovskite semiconductor, allowing First Solar to meet key internal milestones in its perovskite development program, including initial-stage efficiency, stability, and manufacturability objectives,” First Solar notes.

That’s just for starters. By the middle of next year, First Solar expects to have a pilot line up and running at a facility in Ohio, which will apply the technology to its existing Series 6 solar modules.

Recent findings suggest that in addition, last month First Solar unveiled the start of Phase I of operations at its sixth facility in the US. Located in Gaffney, South Carolina, the new factory represents another step in First Solar’s onshoring plan for Series 6 production.

It has been revealed that “The second phase is forecast to be completed by mid-2027, at which time the approximately $330 million facility is expected to double its annual nameplate capacity to 3.4 gigawatts (GW) and produce the Company’s CuRe technology, while supporting nearly 700 jobs. Approximately 500 of those jobs have already been filled,” First Solar explains.

It has been revealed that for the record, the Gaffney facility expands First Solar’s existing footprint in South Carolina. The company also operates in Alabama, Louisiana, and Ohio. All together, First Solar anticipates to have a total of 17 gigawatts’ worth of domestic solar module manufacturing under its belt by the end of this year, which is just around the corner.

Photo: Greenhouse lettuce thrives under natural sunlight filtered through specialized glass from the perovskite solar startup UbiQD, while conserving water resources, too (cropped, courtesy of UbiQD).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Malin Akerman has a private disco in her latest Connecticut home, complete with a mixing deck and a smoke machine.

But ask the star of “The Hunting Wives” where she’s happiest in the house, and she’ll point you to a piece of living room furniture.

“Plopping down on our major pink couch in the living room with my family,” the actress told The Wall Street Journal when he asked about her favorite spot.

According to recent reports, akerman, 48, moved to Connecticut in July with her husband, actor Jack Donnelly, and her son, Sebastian, 13. The family settled into a modern house built in 1988.

“The interior has an inviting flow, and all the rooms are cozy,” she mentioned.

Sources indicate that one room in particular gives her a good excuse to send out invitations. Alongside the DJ equipment, Akerman has a disco ball and a laser. “I love to DJ, dance and have friends over for parties,” she remarked.

Anyone who ever danced at Akerman’s house in Los Angeles might recognize the decor. In May, when she listed her longtime Hollywood Hills home for $2.9 million, she told Elle Decor that her disco ball would be coming east.

Industry observers note that she had a suggestion for whoever bought the place, too. “I sincerely hope the next owners put in a disco ball,” she stated.

According to recent reports, akerman found that California home while working at a downtown L.A. restaurant. A regular learned she was looking for a rental and offered to show her a house he owned with his brother.

She spent three years there as a tenant before buying it in 2008. Over the years, she added a pool and turned the unfinished lower level into a primary suite that opened onto the garden, according to Elle Decor.

Sources indicate that staying at one address for two decades was a departure for Akerman. Her first home was a studio in Stockholm.

In a recent development, when she was 2, her father, Magnus, had job offers in Toronto and New York. Her parents chose Canada, where the view from their townhouse gave their daughter something to do as she drifted off.

“At night, I fell asleep counting trains,” she told the Journal.

According to recent reports, her father returned to Sweden after her parents divorced. Akerman, then 6, stayed in Canada with her mother, Pia.

At 12, she moved into a white house in Niagara-on-the-Lake, the Ontario town where her new stepfather had grown up. Two years later, the marriage ended. Her little brother, Marcus, went to live with his father. Akerman stayed with Pia.

“Given the friction, I don’t have many happy memories of the house,” she remarked.

As she and her mother moved, Akerman changed schools. A drama elective she picked as a high school freshman gave her a circle of friends.

“Drama provided me with community and stability,” she recalled.

When a manager later encouraged her to move to Los Angeles, her best friend, Laura, went with her. A friend from high school took them in.

Acting work was slow to materialize, but Akerman studied the craft, and a role opposite Lisa Kudrow in “The Comeback” helped launch her career.

Industry observers note that now it’s Sebastian who has a role to celebrate at home. Akerman revealed that her son landed a part in Hulu’s “Paradise” on his first audition.

Sources indicate that as for how swiftly he might follow his mother into the family business, she kept her answer brief. “We’re taking it slow.”.

Akerman dates her turning point to her early 20s, when she began to feel confident with her longtime girlfriends in her corner. As she put it, “They made me feel more connected and provided emotional support.”.

Akerman will also soon be celebrating the season 2 premiere of "The Hunting Wives," which airs on Nov. 26.

Key insights from HPE’s Q4 earnings report

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.delivered a record fiscal fourth quarter this week, roughly doubling its fiscal 2027 growth outlook, but its stock gave back nearly all of the prior day’s rally.
  • It has been revealed that fourth-quarter revenue rose 50%, to $14.5 billion, orders grew 88%, and adjusted earnings of $1.43 per share topped the high end of guidance.
  • I joined a briefing with Chief Executive Antonio Neri and a small group of independent analysts shortly before the results came out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:27 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.delivered a record fiscal fourth quarter this week, roughly doubling its fiscal 2027 growth outlook, but its stock gave back nearly all of the prior day’s rally. The selloff suggests Wall Street still prices HPE as a low-margin server vendor, even though the results describe a networking and artificial intelligence infrastructure company with demand exceeding its ability to ship.

It has been revealed that fourth-quarter revenue rose 50%, to $14.5 billion, orders grew 88%, and adjusted earnings of $1.43 per share topped the high end of guidance. HPE now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to grow 27% to 35%, with adjusted earnings of $5.05 to $5.35 per share, according to its earnings release.

I joined a briefing with Chief Executive Antonio Neri and a small group of independent analysts shortly before the results came out. Here are my four takeaways for investors and information technology leaders:.

Neri explained that networking orders grew more than 4.5 times faster than networking revenue in the quarter, up from 3.5 times the quarter before, and HPE exited the year with $10.5 billion in AI backlog.

In a recent development, HPE doubled its networking purchase commitments over the summer and raised them again in the fourth quarter, but those components carry lead times of 28 to 40-plus weeks, so Neri expects networking conversion to pick up starting in the second quarter. Supply constraints are a better problem to have than weak demand, but they mean fiscal 2027 hinges on converting orders rather than winning them.

The Juniper Networks integration is complete, and the annual cost-synergy target has risen to $800 million, but the bigger story remains the profit mix. Chief Financial Officer Marie Myers stated networking will account for more than 40% of HPE’s operating profit by the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, up from less than a quarter of revenue. AI is a major driver, with routing orders growing by triple digits as customers connect AI data centers to one another.

Security was the soft spot, which Neri called “just timing.” When I asked whether the security portfolio is where he wants it as the industry consolidates around significant platforms, he argued for a different path.

“Fortinet and we have a different strategy — the convergence of security and networking — and we are taking it all the way down to the silicon level,” he stated. The convergence of networking and security is underway but will take time to execute, as a considerable amount of technical debt must go through its depreciation cycle. In a greenfield situation, organizations can easily deploy a converged solution, but in a brownfield environment, it requires much more work. This is the right strategy, but it remains a “prove-it” business for HPE.

According to recent reports, many neoclouds rely on vendor financing and chip-backed debt, raising real concerns about who is left exposed if the buildout slows. HPE indicates it has stayed out, and Neri was quite emphatic about it on the briefing.

According to recent reports, “I want to be clear: We have not financed any neocloud through HPFS, our financing arm,” he remarked. “We have zero exposure to any AI financing for neocloud.” HPE has likely left some revenue on the table, but it drew the line in the right place. It will sell to neoclouds, as its $1.2 billion Vultr order shows, without acting as their bank. Enterprise and sovereign customers account for the majority of its cumulative AI orders, and if the neocloud financing chain breaks, HPE’s financing arm won’t be the one holding the paper.

Industry observers note that training built the first phase of AI infrastructure, and Neri believes inference will build the next and will dominate demand for AI infrastructure. “I believe by the end of the decade, 80% will be in AI inferencing,” he stated. “Much of that will land on-prem. Much of that will be distributed, for sure. That’s why the server business is structurally well-positioned.”.

Once agents are in production, token costs become a recurring bill, and companies will want inference running alongside their own data. Those servers require far more memory and pull in storage and services, which is better business than racking graphics processing units for a hyperscaler.

Evidence of this is the interest in Helios, the Advanced Microdevices Inc. rack that uses HPE’s Ethernet switching rather than Nvidia’s proprietary interconnect. I asked Neri whether Jensen Huang’s brief departure from Nvidia Corp. had opened that door. He stated interest was building before then, as customers look to diversify.

It has been revealed that HPE shares jumped 17% on Monday ahead of the report as part of a broader AI rally, then fell about 13% in early trading on Tuesday, ending near where they started the week. I see three reasons for this.

In a recent development, the first is margins. Cloud & AI operating margin was 18.4% in the quarter, and HPE guided to about 14% for fiscal 2027. Reuters reported that JPMorgan analysts called margin mix the key debate for investors.

The second is pricing. Myers said higher selling prices have been the biggest driver of server growth, and she expects gross margin to moderate in the second half as AI server volumes ramp and costs rise faster than pricing.

It has been revealed that the third is timing. HPE expects about 54% of revenue in the second half, with the ramp tied to Helios shipments, the Oracle Corp. deal, customer data center readiness and component supply. Those are fair execution questions, but they miss the shift in where HPE’s profit comes from.

Recent findings suggest that on the topic of margins, the 18.4% came off an unusual stretch of favorable pricing that should not have been modeled as permanent. Neri argued the guide is still “significantly higher than any historical margin we have had in this business,” and he’s right outside the past year. A year ago, the segment’s margin was 9.3%. Margin rate also isn’t margin dollars. At 30% to 40% revenue growth, my math indicates Cloud & AI adding well over $1 billion in operating profit at the midpoint.

In a recent development, the bears are right that price-driven server growth doesn’t warrant a premium multiple, which is why the mix matters more. The market is fixated on the segment whose margins are normalizing and ignoring the one whose margins are expanding. Adjusted earnings per share are still guided to grow by 27% to 35%, in line with revenue growth. That’s far from the margin doom-and-gloom narrative on the stock.

Industry observers note that the back-half concern is real but manageable. Myers described the pipeline as multiples of the backlog, and Neri said the guide assumes only historical win rates against it.

Then there’s quality. HPE is guiding to about 30% growth and at least $5.5 billion in free cash flow, has no neocloud financing exposure and has already brought leverage below its target. It trades at about eight times the midpoint of its adjusted earnings guidance. “I don’t see us at a multiple that is 8 to 9x; it makes no sense whatsoever,” Neri remarked on the earnings call.

For old HPE, that’s true, as it’s a server vendor, but HPE is increasingly a network vendor each quarter. In fact, during our pre-call with Neri, he led with networking and spoke at length about the business before pivoting to the server business. Expect networking to continue to drive a larger share of profits.

Sources indicate that fiscal 2027 is an execution year. HPE must convert purchase commitments into shipments, ramp Helios and prove that networking margins can climb even as cloud and AI margins settle. I’ll be watching networking order conversion more closely than server margins. If HPE executes, today’s multiple will prove to be too low.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Trump administration has agreed to withdraw its moratorium on new broker enrollments, court documents show.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
CMS to withdraw moratorium on new ACA broker registrations" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

In a recent development, UPDATED: Nov 20 at 1:30 p.m. ET.

The Trump administration has agreed to withdraw its moratorium on new broker enrollments, court documents show.

According to a filing submitted Thursday, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Service will published a withdrawal on the Federal Register. The move follows a court ruling earlier this month in favor of two leading organizations representing brokers, which granted a preliminary injunction on the moratorium.

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America both sued over the regulation. NABIP argued that the moratorium would have a significant impact on licensed professionals operating in accordance with the law.

It has been revealed that per the document, that stay will remain in place until CMS publishes its withdrawal notice. Once that has been put forth, the plaintiffs will dismiss their complaints as moot. CMS also agreed not to take further action against agents and brokers during the current open enrollment period.

The moratorium, finalized in September, was a part the agency's broader efforts to root out fraud, waste and abuse on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

UPDATED: Nov. 5 at 4:30 p.m. ET.

A federal court has granted a preliminary injunction to two key groups representing insurance brokers over the Trump administration's moratorium on fresh broker enrollments.

The District Court of Maryland issued the injunction after determining that the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America "have shown that they are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims under the Administrative Procedure Act.".

The court also remarked that the organizations made clear they would likely suffer significant harm if the moratorium stays in place.

In a recent development, NABIP mentioned that the ruling means that it will restart training for new brokers beginning on Nov. 6.

Industry observers note that "Today’s ruling is a significant victory for licensed agents and brokers and the consumers who rely on their expertise," mentioned NABIP President Mychal Walker in an announcement (PDF). "With Open Enrollment already underway, every day matters.".

"Lifting the moratorium immediately and beginning training tomorrow will help affected professionals get to work assisting individuals and families in finding coverage that fits their needs and budgets," noted Walker.

According to recent reports, NABIP initially sued on Oct. 15 to challenge the moratorium. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services instituted the moratorium in late September as part of its broader push to combat fraud on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

PUBLISHED: Oct. 15 at 5:15 p.m. ET.

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals is suing the Trump administration over its moratorium on new brokers entering the Affordable Care Act marketplaces.

The organization, the leading trade group for insurance brokers and agents, stated the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' moratorium impacts close to 19,000 brokers and agents who will be barred from registering ahead of open enrollment.

Industry observers note that CMS unveiled the moratorium in late September as part of its ongoing push to root out fraud, waste and abuse. In addition, the agency stated it would terminate more than 200 agents and brokers that failed to comply with marketplace standards.

The agency stated new brokers and agents were disproportionately responsible for submitting inappropriate enrollments and engaging in behaviors at high risk for fraud.

In an announcement (PDF), NABIP claims that it supports the broader effort to combat fraud, but that CMS' moratorium "threatens the livelihoods of thousands of legitimate, licensed professionals who have not been accused of fraud and limits consumers’ access to professional assistance as they navigate Open Enrollment.".

The organization argues in the lawsuit that the rule instituting the moratorium violates both the Administrative Procedure Act and the Affordable Care Act. The regulation is unlawful as it is "arbitrary, capricious, and unsupported by sufficient evidence," NABIP noted.

The 19,000 agents who would be barred from participating under the rule are part of a critical network of professionals who help consumers find coverage that meets their needs, the organization said.

NABIP President Mychal Walker remarked that CMS should look elsewhere in its fraud efforts.

In a recent development, "The existence of fraud is not in dispute. NABIP has raised these concerns with CMS repeatedly and has offered concrete solutions to address them," Walker stated in the announcement. "What is in dispute is whether the appropriate response is to exclude thousands of legitimate agents based solely on whether they registered last year, without any individualized evidence about them.".

"There is a better approach: target fraud where it occurs, strengthen the system’s security and hold bad actors accountable while preserving consumers’ access to trusted professionals," Walker continued.

CMS has taken steps to crack down on brokers as the agency views improper ACA enrollments as a key target in its fight against fraud. CMS officials have repeatedly raised concerns that people are enrolled in ACA aims without their knowledge, or despite being deceased.

Earlier this week, the agency revealed it will purge 189,000 enrollees who are at the moment listed as enrolled in both ACA plans and other coverage, such as Medicaid or Medicare.

UnitedHealth the latest insurer to sue over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UnitedHealth Group is joining the ranks of insurers that are suing the feds over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings calculations.

Industry observers note that much like other recent lawsuits, the healthcare giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inappropriately used multiple measures in the calculations. Over the summer, a Georgia federal court sided with MA initiative Clover Health, and tossed 20 measures that were used in its 2026 scores.

That legal ruling has been the basis of much of the current round of legal wrangling.

UnitedHealth said in its complaint that it is bringing the lawsuit to ensure "that their 2027 Star Ratings are calculated in accordance with CMS’s statutory authority and procedural obligations.".

Industry observers note that the star ratings are tied to quality bonus payments for Medicare Advantage plans and listed on the Medicare plan finder to help individuals identify high-quality coverage. When those payments are lower due to a decline in scores, the insurer may not be as nimble in lowering premiums or enhancing benefits.

According to recent reports, "The Star Ratings carry real consequences," UnitedHealth wrote in the complaint. "A proposal’s Star Rating thus directly affects the benefits and healthcare offerings that Medicare beneficiaries receive.".

UPDATED: Nov. 9 at 2:30 p.m. ET.

Elevance Health is the latest insurer to sue the feds over its performance in the latest round of star ratings for the Medicare Advantage program.

The company sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in District of Columbia federal court on Friday, arguing that the 2027 star ratings calculations violated the Administrative Procedure Act in using 11 measures that it claims were adopted unlawfully.

In the lawsuit, the tech giant noted that the harm from including these measures is "concrete and substantial." If they were excluded, it would increase the scores for 12 of its Medicare Advantage contracts and generate $516 million in additional quality bonus payments.

Industry observers note that "Their inclusion therefore does more than violate statutory requirements in the abstract: it depresses Elevance Health’s ratings and reduces the funding available for the following payment year," per the lawsuit. "That funding could support broader supplemental benefits, lower premiums and cost-sharing, and improved care coordination.".

"CMS’s unlawful methodology puts those resources out of reach," the company mentioned.

In addition to the financial impacts, Elevance argues that the star ratings scores can also lead to reputational damage that makes it harder for them to compete in the MA market. It also provides prospective enrollees with inaccurate information, the tech giant said.

"Beneficiaries cannot make informed coverage choices when the government’s own comparison tool conveys a distorted assessment of the looks available to them," Elevance mentioned.

It has been revealed that "An artificially depressed rating does not merely place Elevance Health at a competitive disadvantage; it undermines the very comparison the program is supposed to enable," the manufacturer continued. "A rating lowered by unlawful measures presents beneficiaries with a misleading signal of relative quality, rather than a lawful basis for distinguishing among competing plans.".

UPDATED: Oct. 27 at 2:45 p.m. ET.

CVS Heath's Aetna is joining the ranks of insurers suing over its results in the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

The insured filed suit Monday in Georgia's Southern District Court, and argues that 28 measures used by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to calculate its scores were "unlawfully adopted" and should have been excluded.

Recent findings suggest that the court is the same venue that ruled in favor of Clover Health over the summer, and set aside 20 measures that were used to determine its 2026 scores. That decision, which the feds have appealed, kicked off a broad recalculation of 2026 scores that looked different for insurers outside of Clover, triggering a wave of litigation.

In its lawsuit, Aetna cites the Clover decision in finding that CMS extended beyond its statutory authority in deploying those 20 measures.

Sources indicate that the company mentioned that calculating its scores using the 28 measures in question will likely cost it $2 billion in 2028 quality bonus payments and rebate retention. Those are funds that the insurer could "apply toward expanding member benefits, reducing premiums and investing in quality improvement.".

Aetna adds that in addition to the monetary loss, having lower scores negatively impacts the company's reputation and its ability to attract potential members.

"The harm to CVS Health is not exclusively financial; lower ratings carry meaningful reputational harm, which can in turn impact membership," per the lawsuit. "By incorporating unlawful measures into the 2027 Star Ratings calculation, CMS cast CVS Health’s ratings in a poorer light in the eyes of Medicare Advantage consumers relative to peer MAOs, undermining CVS Health’s ability to compete for Medicare beneficiaries through enhanced benefits and the like.".

Aetna did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Sources indicate that based on an analysis from Stephens, 69% of Aetna's MA members are in aims with four or more stars for 2027, down from 81%. That threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments.

Aetna's complaint follows others focused on the 2027 scores from Centene and Alignment Healthcare (see those stories below).

Centene has become the latest insurer to sue the federal government over its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

Recent findings suggest that in a lawsuit filed Thursday in Georgia's Southern District Court, the firm argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services violated the Administrative Procedure Act in determining its latest scores. Centene notes that CMS ran afoul of "core statutory safeguards" in deploying 17 measures.

The use of those measures ultimately caused "significant injury" to the company, according to the complaint. For 2027, 9% of Centene's members are enrolled in plans with at least four stars, which declined from 18% in the prior year.

"In implementing each of the individual Star measures that Centene challenges, CMS violated applicable law and thereby caused Centene to lose out on hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue that Centene could use to strengthen benefits, reduce premiums, and improve health outcomes," the firm mentioned in the lawsuit.

CMS argues that the court has already sided with a similar argument in its decision in favor of Clover Health earlier this year. In that case, which led to a broad recalculation in scores, the courts set aside 20 measures that were used in determining Clover's star ratings for 2026.

If the 17 measures in question had been excluded in calculating Centene's scores, the company estimates it would receive $448 million more in quality bonus payments for the 2028 blueprint year, funds it would deploy to expand benefits, lower premiums and enhance programs like care coordination.

In addition to the financial impact, a drop in star ratings also carries a reputational hit, Centene said.

"Beyond the financial impact to the manufacturer and its members, depressed ratings also inflict significant reputational damage and diminished membership," the company mentioned in the complaint.

Centene had not returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Recent findings suggest that PUBLISHED: Oct. 12 at 3 p.m. ET.

Alignment Healthcare sued federal regulators, alleging that its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings were determined "in flagrant violation" of statute.

In the lawsuit filed Friday in District of Columbia federal court, the insurer says that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services "has completely departed from Congress’s vision of leveraging predictable, valid measures developed with input from providers, plans, and the public" in establishing the methodology for the star ratings.

The company argues that rather than establish "consistent, stable specifications" for metrics through the traditional rule-making process, the agency instead detailed key measures through a series of "technical notes." This violates the Administrative Procedure Act, per the lawsuit.

The program's star ratings are the critical determinant in quality bonus payments to insurers as well as a tool that aims to make it easier for enrollees and brokers to identify benefits with the highest quality.

"Consistent application of the statutory requirements governing Star Ratings is therefore essential not only to plan payments and competition but also to ensuring that beneficiaries can rely on the Star Ratings as meaningful and comparable measures of plan quality," Alignment stated in the lawsuit.

The company adds that multiple recent court decisions have set aside CMS' star ratings methodology, notably a ruling over the summer in favor of Clover Health that tossed 20 metrics used in the 2026 calculations. A Georgia federal judge determined that 10 measures utilized exceeded CMS' authority, while 10 other measures were promulgated inappropriately.

CMS recalculated the scores across the board following the ruling, but only set aside the 10 measures that the courts determined were outside the bounds of its regulatory authority. The agency maintained that approach in the 2027 calculations, Alignment argues.

Recent findings suggest that "Congress created the Star Ratings program to allow Medicare Advantage beneficiaries to make informed decisions about plan enrollment based on clinically validated measures of plan quality that had been subjected to notice and comment," the organization said. "CMS’s contrary approach fails to carry out the vision that Congress set forth by statute.".

The Trump administration has appealed the Clover decision, so that legal case remains ongoing.

According to recent reports, in addition, Alignment argues it suffered reputational and financial damage as a result of its 2027 scores, which plummeted compared to the prior year. Just 25% of its members are in plans with four or more stars for 2027, down from 100% in 2026.

Shares in the company tumbled following the release of the ratings, though stock prices have rebounded since.

Alignment sued the feds following the Clover decision to secure a recalculation for its scores that aligns with the court's decision, and in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, mentioned that the lawsuit aligns with that perspective.

"Our lawsuit seeks to ensure that the Star Ratings program operates as Congress intended and that Alignment is properly compensated for the care we provide," Alignment mentioned in the statement. "We respect the judicial process and will present our case in court. Because this matter involves pending litigation, we will not comment on the specific legal arguments beyond our filings.".

"Our focus remains on delivering exceptional care, improving health outcomes and advocating for a stable, lawful regulatory framework that supports seniors and strengthens the Medicare Advantage program," the company noted.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Unfortunately, it’s also the prime time for an oven fire.
  • In a recent development, moneyGeek recently analyzed seven years of fire department reports to the National Fire Incident Reporting System and compared each state's Thanksgiving Day cooking fires with its own average November day, from 2019 to 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let’s face it: The holiday season is when our ovens are working overtime.

Unfortunately, it’s also the prime time for an oven fire.

In a recent development, moneyGeek recently analyzed seven years of fire department reports to the National Fire Incident Reporting System and compared each state's Thanksgiving Day cooking fires with its own average November day, from 2019 to 2025. Nationally, departments reported 3.72 times as many residential cooking fires on Thanksgiving.

And it's not just the turkey that could get ruined.

While a professional kitchen remodel averages $26,994, depending on the scope of the project and the location, according to Angi.com, fire damage might amp up that pricetag depending on whether cabinets, drywall, appliances, or partial finishes need to be removed and replaced.

Major structural damage can reach $100,000 if flames or water damaged wiring and plumbing or if the fire spread to adjacent rooms.

This is why experts recommend tried and true precautions homeowners can take to keep their home safe.

In the days leading up to the holidays, be sure to inspect the inside of your oven.

“Look specifically for older grease buildups,” notes Steve Lockwood, owner of Mountain State Fire Protection, a fire safety equipment inspector and installer in Mesa, AZ.

“Over time, those can build up, become extremely hot, and they could ignite pretty easily.”.

If you’re someone who routinely stores items in your oven, be sure to empty the space entirely—before you preheat it.

“Often people don’t realize they have plastic cutting boards and casserole dishes with plastic lids stored in their oven,” Sam Taylor, disaster public affairs program manager with the American Red Cross, tells Realtor.com.

“You don’t want to run the risk of melting those items in the oven.”.

During the entire time you’re cooking a dish on your burners, stow all combustible materials away.

“Pay special attention to such items as plastic spatulas and utensils that can melt and catch fire, as well as wooden spoons, oven mitts, and paper products,” Taylor says.

Always make sure you’re not cooking foods on too-high temperatures, which can result in a fire; avoid dangerous bump-ins; and make sure pan handles don’t hang over the edge of the burners.

Industry observers note that “This can cause the contents to spill and could cause burns or fire,” Lockwood says. And never wear a shirt with long, loose sleeves while you’re cooking.

Sources indicate that “If you’re working over an open flame, that sleeve can catch fire,” states Taylor. “I always recommend wearing a different top that doesn’t have any fabric hanging near a flame.”.

Whatever you do, never leave the house when your oven is on, Lockwood says.

“Where most people go wrong is walking away from the kitchen,” he says. Instead, keep an eye on your oven at all times. Tip: If you have a newer digital stove, pay special attention.

Industry observers note that “A lot of these burners can be accidentally turned on just by leaning over them,” Lockwood notes. “That’s why it’s a good practice to put the stove into a lockout mode to avoid an accidental turn on.”.

Should a fire happen, keep the oven door closed, turn off the heat, reach for your kitchen extinguisher, and alert the authorities.

“Opening the oven door feeds the fire with oxygen,” Lockwood says. “In addition, while baking soda will work in a pinch, never use water on a grease fire.”.

And, if a pot on your burner catches fire, turn off the heat and put a lid or baking sheet on it immediately to smother the fire, he adds.

Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (657 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open latest possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders.
  • In a recent development, the findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins.
  • Mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open latest possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders. Researchers found that the vitamin can correct developmental problems in tiny worms carrying a genetic mutation associated with Verheij syndrome, a rare human condition that causes developmental delays, impaired growth, and short stature.

In a recent development, the findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins. During splicing, unnecessary portions of messenger RNA are removed, and the remaining sections are joined together in the correct order. When this process goes wrong, it can disrupt essential cellular functions and contribute to serious developmental disorders.

Mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome. To better understand the effects of these genetic changes, scientists investigated how a related mutation affects growth and metabolism in a laboratory model.

Vitamin B12 Reverses Developmental Defects in Worms.

The discovery emerged from experiments involving C. elegans, a tiny roundworm commonly used in biological research. The researchers were initially searching for previously unknown genes that influence lifespan when they began examining a mutation in a gene involved in RNA splicing. The same gene is associated with Verheij syndrome in humans.

Worms carrying the mutation developed problems resembling crucial features of the human disorder. Their growth slowed considerably, and they remained smaller than normal.

Sources indicate that to investigate why this happened, the scientists conducted genetic screens and analyzed the worms' metabolism. They discovered that the mutation disrupted specific metabolic pathways that depend on vitamin B12 and are essential for healthy growth and normal cellular activity.

Industry observers note that the researchers then tested whether providing additional vitamin B12 could counteract these changes. Remarkably, the treatment restored the affected metabolic processes to normal and corrected the developmental abnormalities associated with the mutation.

"We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism," says Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. "Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12.".

Could Vitamin B12 Help Treat a Rare Genetic Disorder?

To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the researchers examined publicly available datasets from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at the University Hospital Cologne, to collect blood samples from patients diagnosed with Verheij syndrome.

These investigations uncovered evidence of similar metabolic changes in humans, suggesting that the vitamin B12-related pathways affected in the worms may also play a role in the human disorder.

Although the results are promising, researchers have not yet established whether vitamin B12 supplementation can improve symptoms in people with Verheij syndrome. Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether the benefits observed in worms can be translated into a treatment for patients.

Industry observers note that the discovery also raises a broader possibility. Metabolic disruptions may contribute more substantially to diseases caused by faulty RNA splicing than scientists previously recognized. Understanding these connections could help researchers identify newly introduced therapeutic strategies, potentially extending beyond Verheij syndrome to other rare genetic conditions.

"Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide latest insights into human diseases," indicates Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. "A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term.".

CMS issues Medicare Advantage proposals aimed at boosting competition" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has proposed a slew of changes to Medicare Advantage and Part D designed to "revitalize care" in these markets.

For one, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said late Friday that it will update application and network adequacy requirements to make it easier for newly introduced entrants. The agency proposed to require organizations to demonstrate network adequacy during their first year in operation, rather than during the application process.

This shift would eliminate a significant barrier for upcoming entrants, driving greater competition in the market.

It has been revealed that CMS has also proposed combining three specialty areas in behavioral health—clinical psychology, clinical social work and outpatient behavioral health—into one specialty group for the purposes of network adequacy. The changes will give looks greater flexibility in building out behavioral health networks.

CMS will also make adjustments that seek to boost competition for special needs plans.

Sources indicate that in addition, the agency said it will make adjustments to the star ratings program, focusing its ratings on 15 measures. The proposed measure set would emphasize "clinical outcomes and patient experience while retaining select process measures in high-priority areas where performance remains low.".

CMS is also aiming to update the calculation methodology that will "raise the bar for achieving high ratings," and thus quality bonus payments.

"People with Medicare should be able to choose coverage based on what matters most to them—quality, affordability and access," noted CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These proposals are about creating a Medicare Advantage marketplace that rewards better care and better value while empowering beneficiaries with the options and knowledge they need to make informed decisions about their health.".

The proposed rule also includes provisions that align with Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again agenda by setting a "healthy food" standard that MA plans should follow for supplemental benefits.

The goal, CMS mentioned, is to ensure that Medicare dollars are spent on food benefits that align with MAHA.

"Medicare food benefits should pay for nutritious food that helps people improve their health and manage chronic disease," Kennedy noted in the announcement. "This proposal would require those benefits to meet the Dietary Guidelines for Americans while preserving access to foods and nutritional products that providers recommend for patients’ specific medical needs.".

"Under President Trump, we are putting prevention at the center of health care and demanding more from every Medicare dollar," Kennedy stated.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are criticizing Nvidia Corp.’s decision to rehire Jensen Huang as its chief executive.

The criticism came against the backdrop of a controversial move by the U.S. Commerce Department. The agency applied new export restrictions to Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud operator. The company played a prominent role in the spy controversy that led to Huang’s resignation. According to trade experts, the Commerce Department left out a key clause that is usually included in such restrictions.

Huang resigned on Nov. 12 following revelations that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. Early reporting about the relationship indicated that she was found to have passed intelligence to China. The U.S. Justice Department later stated that it has not yet reached a conclusion on whether Alice Huang is a spy. Earlier this week, the Newly introduced York Times reported that she maintained contact with a Chinese intelligence official.

Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang on Monday after U.S. President Donald Trump and tech industry figures urged directors to bring him back. The move drew widespread criticism from members of Congress.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York), who is set to become House Speaker, called the reinstatement “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.” Rep. Don Bacon (R-Nebraska), the chair of House Subcommittee on Cyber, Information Technologies and Innovation, stated that “it’s inexplicable to me why they want this guy back as CEO.” Former Utah Republican Senator and Massachusetts Governor Mitt Romney tweeted: “Let me get this straight: we rushed AI along without regulating safeguards in order to stay ahead of China and at the same time, we sold China the very chips they’d need to get ahead of us. Smells of profit, corruption and perhaps worse.”.

Industry observers note that multiple lawmakers told CNBC that they initiative to scrutinize Huang’s conduct closely. The executive is scheduled to testify before multiple Congressional committees next Tuesday. Furthermore, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon) told the outlet that Democrats plan to scrutinize the Trump administration’s role in the matter.

The Commerce Department today added Megaspeed and several of its regional affiliates to its Entity List. Companies on the list can only purchase sensitive products such as graphics cards if they obtain a license from the U.S. government. According to Gizmodo, the move has drawn scrutiny because the restrictions applied to Megaspeed include a loophole.

It has been revealed that all the companies on the Entity List are prohibited from buying Nvidia’s latest chips unless they secure a license. Most of them are also unable to buy lower-end graphics cards, high-bandwidth memory and related hardware. The latter restrictions are specified in a clause called the FDPR provision. The Commerce Department has reportedly not applied the FDPR provision to Megaspeed when it added the firm to the Entity List.

Sources indicate that huang returned to Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters on Monday. The news sent the chipmaker’s stock soaring more than 30%, although it parred some of the gains today. Nvidia shares are down 5.8% from Monday.

Wired today published excerpts from Huang’s all-hands meeting with employees. The executive apologized for his affairs and for his management style, which has also come under scrutiny in recent days. He added that he will undergo a “360-degree review” and that Nvidia’s code of conduct is still in effect.
